title: Living What We Say Is True
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer's monthly letter to leaders argues that speaking truth is not enough unless it becomes integrated into how leaders act, relate and decide. She locates most tension in people and organisations in the gap between stated values and lived behaviour, and says that gap usually reflects the difficulty of living what we know rather than hypocrisy. Integrity, in her framing, is not perfection but the outcome of sustained truth-telling over time, so truth must be a daily practice rather than a single courageous act. For leaders the practice is visible: people watch how they handle discomfort, set boundaries and keep commitments, and trust builds through consistency and congruence, which she calls Alignment of Purpose in her Leadership Connection Model. The essay opens with a reflection on current political and social conditions and ends with reflection questions, so its leadership core is a compact argument that truth lived over time becomes trust. The tone is exhortatory and values-driven rather than evidence-based.
points: Most tension in individuals, organisations and communities comes from the gap between stated values and daily behaviour, which is usually difficulty rather than hypocrisy.
Integrity is reframed as the natural result of sustained truth-telling rather than perfection.
Speaking truth must be a daily practice that includes noticing when we are avoiding, rushing or outsourcing responsibility.
Leaders are watched closely for how they handle discomfort, boundaries, commitments and hard decisions, so trust comes from congruence rather than vision statements.
Truth lived over time becomes trust, which in turn lets others offer honesty and courage of their own.
quotes: Most of the tension we experience, in ourselves, in organizations, in communities, comes from the gap between our stated values and our lived behavior. We say we value integrity, equity, collaboration, or care, yet our daily choices often tell a more complicated story.

Integrity, then, is not perfection. It is the natural outcome of sustained truth-telling over time. When we continue to acknowledge what is real and allow it to inform our decisions, we begin to align our actions with our values, one choice at a time.

This is why speaking truth must be understood as a daily practice, not a single courageous moment. Truth asks us to pay attention. To notice when we are avoiding, rushing, or outsourcing responsibility.
People watch how leaders handle discomfort, set boundaries, follow through on commitments, and make decisions when no option is easy. Trust is not built through declarations or vision statements.
It is built slowly, through consistency and congruence when what we say and what we do begin to match. In the Leadership Connection Model, we call it Alignment of Purpose.
Said simply, truth lived over time becomes trust. And trust, once established, creates the conditions for others to step forward with honesty, creativity, and courage of their own.
